caption.text: Human figures ride stylized leopards around this painted wooden seat. Cleveland attributes it to a Babanki-style maker in the Cameroon Grassfields. Such chairs helped mark kingships and also circulated as royal gifts and works for local or European patrons. Authority is carried through supports, animal imagery and the act of sitting.

proposals.reason: The theme explicitly includes authority represented through material, posture, costume and symbols. This exact chair's primary record explains its kingship and royal-gift functions; exceptional anthropological and sculptural significance is specific, rather than inferred from ordinary utility.

caption.text: This silver reliquary gives a container for saints’ relics the shape of the Holy Sepulchre. Its small architectural body links sacred remains to a place associated with Christ’s burial. Historical accounts identify its contents differently; the building-shaped container gives devotion a visible form.

proposals.reason: The theme concerns specific religious, ceremonial and commemorative purposes. The exact museum record identifies the reliquary form, relic-container use and disagreement over its contents.

caption.text: Wyspiański painted white lilies on the pale blue panels of this wooden casket. Dark framing separates the plant compositions while the flowers repeat across front, back and sides. Turn the box to follow how a flat painted motif changes the character of a solid wooden volume.

proposals.reason: The theme includes paint and shallow surface work as essential meaning. The primary description specifies the pale blue ground, white lilies, dark framing and repetition on the individual faces; the maker's decoration is central to this object.

caption.text: Raised ceramic forms turn an image into an uneven surface. Książek set the glazed panel in cement within a metal frame; the museum relates the series to urban architecture and church towers. Moving around the relief changes how its lines, shadows and colored glazes divide the composition.

proposals.reason: The exact primary record connects ceramic relief, glaze, cement support and metal frame with a series responding to architecture. This brings a modern ceramic method into the exhibition's comparison of depth, surface and ornament.

caption.text: This detached sandstone head comes from a deva at Preah Khan in Angkor. Its five-tiered lotus tiara and modeled face preserve part of a larger figure connected with the Churning of the Ocean of Milk. The head can be examined in detail, while the figure’s body, companions and architectural setting require other evidence.

proposals.reason: The theme explicitly includes isolated heads and loss of original context. Cleveland identifies the exact head, Preah Khan origin, five-tiered tiara and mythic narrative; the caption distinguishes surviving part from missing context without asserting the lost body's fate.

caption.text: A Chinese guardian lion lies on its back, holding a ball that supports a cub. The ball is the ink container. The arrangement turns a protective animal image into an elaborate object for writing, with cloisonné and champlevé color carried across the metal surface. Look for how the adult and cub organize the vessel.

proposals.reason: The theme explicitly compares animals as vessels and guardians. The exact record describes the inverted adult, ball-shaped ink container, cub and both enamel techniques; the caption makes the unusual sculptural function concrete.

caption.text: A city’s authority fits inside this ring. Its gold hoop bears the date 1532, while the museum records a replacement sapphire bought in 1590. Kraków’s arms are cut into the stone so the civic insignia could also serve as a seal. The object joins public office, precious material and an image made to leave an impression.

proposals.reason: Civic insignia and an operational seal make authority material; preserves the documented replacement rather than treating the complete ring as unchanged in1532.

caption.text: A pillar surrounded by flames marks the Buddha’s presence in this limestone panel from Nagarjunakonda. Attendants hold fly whisks beside it; above, celestial beings praise another miraculous pillar. Sacred presence is conveyed through radiance, symbols and acts of veneration rather than a standing human figure.

proposals.reason: A specific Buddhist devotional image broadens the exhibition’s comparison of religious form and purpose without merging traditions.

caption.text: A Maya ballplayer dives toward a rubber ball, his padded torso prepared for impact. The stepped walls probably mark a ball court. Move around the vessel to find the scene: a curved ceramic surface holds a selected instant of bodily movement. Cleveland records that this vessel was repaired after breaking into 34 pieces.

proposals.reason: The source explicitly describes a diving player and impact protection, matching the exhibition’s selected moments and bodily balance; the ceramic support and conserved state remain explicit.

caption.text: An ivory panel carved around 1000 sits inside a fourteenth-century jeweled setting. Scenes of the Wedding at Cana survive within a later book-shaped reliquary made to hold gospel leaves and saints’ relics. The object joins work from different periods; its present form should not be assigned wholly to the ivory carver or to one date.

proposals.reason: Historical reuse and a later setting make the exhibition’s changes-of-use theme concrete; preserves component chronology and qualified attribution.

caption.text: These gilt-bronze pillars once supported a stupa at Tibet’s Densatil Monastery. Bodhisattvas faced visitors, while offering goddesses faced inward toward the monument. A Tibetan syllable marked each support’s place in the larger structure. Turning the surviving objects reveals both sides, but the tiered sacred monument that organized their original viewing is absent.

proposals.reason: Separately recorded architectural supports preserve both decorated sides while losing the organizing monument; avoids inventing a full digital reconstruction or a destruction narrative.

caption.text: A bat perches on the sleeping poet Li Taibo’s shoulder, while a deer nestles behind him. Cleveland connects the bat with good fortune and the deer with longevity and prosperity. Carved into a small piece of amber, the animals give a human figure an auspicious setting. Turn the group to find how they fit around the poet and his wine jar.

proposals.reason: Animals carry specific cultural meanings within a compact Chinese carving, extending the exhibition beyond freestanding animal bodies without flattening the symbolism into a universal claim.
